sections.b: Polycarp's only surviving letter answers a request from Philippi. It praises the church for escorting Ignatius and other prisoners (1:1; 9:1), teaches each group in the church its duties (4:2-6:3), warns against those who deny that Christ came in the flesh (7:1), grieves over a fallen elder, Valens (11:1-4), and sends copies of Ignatius's letters (13:2). It is woven from the words of the New Testament letters, above all 1 Peter, Paul and 1 John, and it calls Polycarp nothing but one of the elders (1:0). The Greek is lost after 9:2 except for chapter 13, which Eusebius quotes; the rest survives in Latin.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 1:0; Polycarp to the Philippians 3:2; Polycarp to the Philippians 7:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2

sections.b: The Philippians had welcomed Ignatius in chains and walked him on his way (1:1), and Polycarp sets 'the blessed Ignatius, Zosimus and Rufus' beside Paul as examples of endurance (9:1). Both the Philippians and Ignatius had asked Polycarp to send their letters to Antioch, as Ignatius asked the churches in his letters (13:1; Ignatius, To Polycarp 7-8). In 13:2 Polycarp asks for news of Ignatius, which led P. N. Harrison (1936) to argue that chapter 13 was written before chapters 1-12, where Ignatius is already 'with the Lord' (9:2) (see the chapter pages).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 1:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 9:1-2; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:1-2

sections.b: Polycarp's letter shows the church at Philippi two generations after Paul. It still remembers Paul, who taught there 'face to face' and wrote to it (3:2; 11:3); it is led by elders and deacons (5:3); it cares for widows (4:3); it welcomed Ignatius and other prisoners on the road through Macedonia to Rome (1:1); and it is shaken by the fall of an elder, Valens, through greed (11:1-4).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 1:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 3:2; Polycarp to the Philippians 11:1-4; Acts 16:12

sections.b: Polycarp writes to the same church as Paul and uses Paul's words to it: 'live as citizens worthy' (5:2; Philippians 1:27), 'did not run for nothing' (9:2; Philippians 2:16), 'the enemies of the cross' (12:3; Philippians 3:18). He speaks of Paul's 'letters' to the Philippians (3:2), plural, and in the Latin of 11:3 of the beginning of 'his letter'. Whether he knew more than one letter is uncertain.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 3:2; Polycarp to the Philippians 5:2; Polycarp to the Philippians 9:2; Polycarp to the Philippians 11:3; Philippians 1:27; Philippians 2:16; Philippians 3:18

sections.b: Polycarp calls him 'blessed and glorious Paul', whose wisdom no one 'like me' can follow (3:2), counts him among those whose endurance the Philippians saw (9:1), and cites him by name, 'as Paul teaches' (11:2). His letter draws on Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, 2 Thessalonians and 1 and 2 Timothy.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 3:2; Polycarp to the Philippians 9:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 11:2-3

sections.b: Polycarp writes for 'the elders with him' (1:0) and says that when Paul praised the Philippians, 'we had not yet come to know' the Lord (11:3): the church of Smyrna came later than Paul's churches in Macedonia. Ignatius had written from Smyrna, and Polycarp kept copies of his letters there (13:2).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 1:0; Polycarp to the Philippians 11:3; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2; Revelation 2:8-11

sections.b: Polycarp names only elders and deacons as leaders, and tells the church to submit to them 'as to God and Christ' (5:3). He never names an overseer, though later writers call him the overseer of Smyrna. His picture of an elder is a pastor: bringing back strays, visiting the sick, caring for widows, orphans and the poor, slow to believe a charge and gentle in judgment (6:1). The one elder he names, Valens, fell through greed (11:1).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 1:0; Polycarp to the Philippians 5:3; Polycarp to the Philippians 6:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 11:1

sections.h: Deacons, servants of the servant of all
sections.b: Deacons must be blameless, not double-tongued, not lovers of money, 'as deacons of God and Christ', living by the truth of the Lord, 'who became the servant of all' (5:2), the same Greek word, diakonos. Many of their qualities match 1 Timothy 3:8-13.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 5:2; Polycarp to the Philippians 5:3; 1 Timothy 3:8-13

sections.b: Polycarp calls the church's widows 'God's altar' (4:3): they pray for everyone without stopping, and like offerings they are 'checked for blemishes', so they must keep away from slander and greed.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 4:3; 1 Timothy 5:3-16

sections.h: Love of money in Polycarp's letter
sections.b: 'Love of money is where every trouble begins' (4:1, after 1 Timothy 6:10). Polycarp warns every group against it (2:2; 4:3; 5:2; 6:1), and the reason appears in chapter 11: an elder at Philippi, Valens, had fallen through greed, which Polycarp calls idolatry (11:2).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 4:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 11:1-2; 1 Timothy 6:10

common: Polycarp's warnings against the love of money are aimed at the case of Valens (11:1-2).

sections.b: 'When you can do good, do not delay, because "alms rescue from death"' (10:2). The saying is Tobit's (Tobit 4:10; 12:9), given without a formula as a known truth. The verse survives only in Latin.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 10:2; Tobit 4:10; Tobit 12:9

sections.h: An antichrist: whoever denies the flesh
sections.b: 'Everyone who does not confess Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is an antichrist' (7:1). Polycarp joins 1 John 4:2-3 and 2 John 7 and applies the word to any teacher who denies that Christ had a real body.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 7:1; 1 John 4:2-3; 2 John 7

sections.b: Polycarp names no false teacher but gives three marks: they deny Christ came in the flesh, do not confess the testimony of the cross, and twist the Lord's sayings to deny resurrection and judgment (7:1). His answer is to return 'to the word that was passed on to us at the start' (7:2). Irenaeus says Polycarp later called Marcion 'the first-born of Satan'.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 6:3; Polycarp to the Philippians 7:1-2

sections.b: 'The one who raised him from the dead will raise us too, if we do his will' (2:2, after 2 Corinthians 4:14). Polycarp counts denial of the resurrection as the mark of 'the firstborn of Satan' (7:1).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 2:1-2; Polycarp to the Philippians 7:1; 2 Corinthians 4:14

sections.b: Christ 'is coming as judge of the living and the dead' (2:1), 'every one of us must stand at Christ's judgment seat' (6:2), and 'the saints will judge the world' (11:2, from 1 Corinthians 6:2).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 2:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 6:2; Polycarp to the Philippians 11:2

sections.b: Before he became a martyr himself, Polycarp held up Ignatius, Zosimus and Rufus, others from Philippi, Paul and the apostles as examples: they 'ran in faith and righteousness' and are 'in the place owed to them, with the Lord' (9:1-2). Their chains are 'crowns' (1:1), and Christ's endurance is 'the model to trace' (8:2).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 1:1; Polycarp to the Philippians 8:2; Polycarp to the Philippians 9:1-2

sections.b: Polycarp gives duties to wives, widows, deacons, younger men, virgins and elders in turn (4:2-6:1), like the New Testament household codes but organized around church groups, with nothing on slaves or masters.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 4:2-6:1; Ephesians 5:22-6:9; 1 Timothy 5:3-16

sections.b: Polycarp quotes Ephesians 2: 'it is by grace that you have been saved, not from works, but by the will of God through Jesus Christ' (1:3).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 1:3; Ephesians 2:8-9

sections.b: Polycarp says believers are saved 'by grace ... not from works' (1:3) and that God will raise us 'if we do his will' (2:2). He sees no tension; later debates over faith and works read such pairings differently.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 1:3; Polycarp to the Philippians 2:2; Ephesians 2:8-10

sections.b: 'Pray also for kings, for authorities and rulers, for those who persecute you and hate you, and for the enemies of the cross' (12:3). Lake's footnote: 'kings' renders the Greek title regularly used of the emperor.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 12:3; 1 Timothy 2:1-2

sections.b: Polycarp's letter is in no church's Bible. It matters for the history of the canon because it uses so many New Testament writings, and in one place, in Latin, introduces Ephesians 4:26 (with Psalm 4) as 'these Scriptures' (12:1). Jerome says it was still read in the churches of Asia in his day (Lives of Illustrious Men 17).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 12:1; Ephesians 4:26; 2 Peter 3:16

sections.b: Eusebius noticed that Polycarp 'made use of certain testimonies drawn from the First Epistle of Peter' (Church History 4.14.9). Among them: 'a joy that words cannot tell, a joy made glorious' (1:3; 1 Peter 1:8), 'tuck up your robes' (2:1; 1 Peter 1:13), the sinless Christ who carried our sins onto the tree (8:1; 1 Peter 2:22-24), the 'model to trace' (8:2; 1 Peter 2:21), and good conduct among the Gentiles (10:2; 1 Peter 2:12).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 1:3; Polycarp to the Philippians 8:1-2; Polycarp to the Philippians 10:2; 1 Peter 2:21-24

sections.b: Polycarp tells the Philippians to treat their fallen elder Valens and his wife not 'as enemies' but to 'call them back as members who can be hurt and who have wandered', praying for their true repentance (11:4, after 2 Thessalonians 3:15 and 2 Timothy 2:25).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 11:4; 2 Thessalonians 3:15; 2 Timothy 2:25

sections.b: Polycarp 2:3 gives 'Do not judge' in Matthew 7:1's exact Greek, 'Forgive' and 'Show mercy' in a form no Gospel has but 1 Clement 13:2 shares, and two beatitudes joined from Luke and Matthew. It shows how a Christian of Asia used the Lord's sayings.
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 2:3; Matthew 7:1-2; Luke 6:36-38; 1 Clement 13:2

sections.b: Polycarp's one surviving letter, to the church at Philippi, is a short pastoral letter woven from the New Testament letters and sent as a covering letter with copies of Ignatius's letters (13:2). Its Greek survives only to 9:2 and in chapter 13, which Eusebius quotes; the rest is known from an old Latin translation (Lake).
sections.refs: Polycarp to the Philippians 1:0; Polycarp to the Philippians 13:2
